title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: From Smolensk the troops continued to retreat, with the enemy in pursuit. On the tenth of August the regiment Prince Andrew commanded was marching along the highway past the avenue leading to Bald Hills. Heat and drought had continued for more than three weeks. Each day fluffy clouds floated across the sky and occasionally veiled the sun, but toward evening the sky cleared again and the sun set in reddish-brown mist. Heavy night dews alone refreshed the earth. The unharvested grain was scorched and shedding its seeds. The marshes dried up. The cattle lowed from hunger, finding no food on the sun-parched meadows. Only at night and in the forests, while the dew lasted, was there any freshness. But on the road—the highway along which the troops marched—there was no freshness even at night or when the road passed through forest; the dew was imperceptible on the sandy dust churned up more than six inches deep. As soon as day dawned, the march began. The artillery and baggage wagons moved silently through the deep dust that rose to the very wheel hubs, and the infantry sank ankle-deep in that soft, choking, hot dust that never cooled even at night. Some of this dust was kneaded by feet and wheels, while the rest rose and hung like a cloud over the troops, settling in eyes, ears, hair, and nostrils, and worst of all in the lungs of men and animals as they moved along that road. The higher the sun rose, the higher rose that cloud of dust, and through the screen of its hot fine particles one could look with the naked eye at the sun, which showed like a huge crimson ball in the unclouded sky. There was no wind, and the men choked in that motionless air. They marched with handkerchiefs tied over their noses and mouths. When they passed through a village, they all rushed to the wells and fought for the water, drinking it down to the mud.

Prince Andrew was in command of a regiment, and the management of that regiment—the welfare of the men and the necessity of receiving and giving orders—absorbed him entirely. The burning of Smolensk and its abandonment marked an epoch in his life. A new feeling of anger against the enemy made him forget his own sorrow. He devoted himself entirely to the affairs of his regiment and was considerate and kind to his men and officers. In the regiment they called him "our prince," were proud of him, and loved him. But he was kind and gentle only to those of his regiment, to Timokhin and the like—people completely new to him, belonging to a different world, who could not know or understand his past. As soon as he encountered a former acquaintance or anyone from the staff, he bristled up at once and became spiteful, ironic, and contemptuous. Everything that reminded him of his past was repugnant to him, and so in his relations with that former world he confined himself to trying to do his duty and not be unfair.

In truth, everything presented itself in a dark and gloomy light to Prince Andrew, especially after the abandonment of Smolensk on the sixth of August (he believed it could and should have been defended) and after his sick father had been forced to flee to Moscow, leaving his beloved Bald Hills—which he had built and populated—to be plundered. But despite this, thanks to his regiment, Prince Andrew had something to think about that was entirely separate from general questions. Two days earlier he had received news that his father, son, and sister had left for Moscow; and though there was nothing for him to do at Bald Hills, Prince Andrew, with a characteristic desire to aggravate his own grief, decided he had to ride there.

He ordered his horse saddled and, leaving his regiment on the march, rode to his father's estate where he had been born and spent his childhood. Riding past the pond where there had always been dozens of women chattering as they rinsed their laundry or beat it with wooden paddles, Prince Andrew noticed there wasn't a soul about, and the little washing dock, torn from its place and half submerged, was floating on its side in the middle of the pond. He rode to the gatekeeper's lodge. No one was at the stone entrance gates of the drive and the door was open. Grass had already begun to grow on the garden paths, and horses and calves were wandering through the English park. Prince Andrew rode up to the greenhouse; some of the glass panes were broken, and some of the trees in tubs were overturned, others dried up. He called for Taras the gardener, but no one replied. Having gone around the corner of the greenhouse to the ornamental garden, he saw that the carved garden fence was broken and branches of the plum trees had been torn off with the fruit. An old peasant whom Prince Andrew had often seen at the gate in his childhood was sitting on a green garden seat, weaving a bast shoe.

He was deaf and didn't hear Prince Andrew ride up. He was sitting on the bench the old prince used to like to sit on, and beside him strips of bast were hanging on the broken and withered branch of a magnolia.

Prince Andrew rode up to the house. Several lime trees in the old garden had been cut down, and a piebald mare and her foal were wandering among the rosebushes in front of the house. The shutters were all closed except at one open window. A little servant boy, seeing Prince Andrew, ran into the house. Alpatych, having sent his family away, was alone at Bald Hills, sitting indoors reading the Lives of the Saints. On hearing that Prince Andrew had come, he went out with his spectacles on his nose, buttoning his coat, and hastily stepping up, without a word began weeping and kissing Prince Andrew's knee.

Then, vexed at his own weakness, he turned away and began reporting on the state of affairs. Everything precious and valuable had been moved to Bogucharovo. Seventy quarters of grain had also been carted away. The hay and the spring grain, of which Alpatych said there had been a remarkable crop that year, had been commandeered by the troops and mowed down while still green. The peasants were ruined; some had also gone to Bogucharovo, and only a few remained.
Without waiting to hear him finish, Prince Andrew asked:
"When did my father and sister leave?"—meaning when did they leave for Moscow.

Alpatych, understanding the question to be about their departure for Bogucharovo, replied that they had left on the seventh, and again went into details about the estate management, asking for instructions.
"Should I let the troops have the oats and take a receipt? We still have six hundred quarters left," he asked.

"What can I tell him?" thought Prince Andrew, looking down at the old man's bald head shining in the sun and seeing from his expression that the old man himself understood how out of place these questions were and only asked them to ease his grief.
"Yes, let them have it," replied Prince Andrew.

"If you noticed some disorder in the garden," said Alpatych, "it was impossible to prevent. Three regiments came through and spent the night—dragoons, mostly. I took down the name and rank of their commanding officer so I could file a complaint."
"Well, what are you going to do? Stay here if the enemy occupies the place?" asked Prince Andrew.
Alpatych turned his face to Prince Andrew, looked at him, and suddenly with a solemn gesture raised his arm.
"He is my refuge! His will be done!" he exclaimed.
A group of bareheaded peasants was approaching across the meadow toward the prince.
"Well, goodbye!" said Prince Andrew, bending down to Alpatych. "You must leave too—take away what you can, and tell the serfs to go to the Ryazan estate or to the one near Moscow."
Alpatych clung to Prince Andrew's leg and burst into sobs. Gently freeing himself, the prince spurred his horse and galloped down the avenue.

The old man was still sitting in the ornamental garden, like a fly sitting motionless on the face of a loved one who is dead, tapping the shoe last on which he was weaving the bast shoe, and two little girls, running out from the greenhouse carrying plums they had picked in their skirts, came upon Prince Andrew. Seeing the young master, the older one seized her younger companion by the hand with a frightened look and hid with her behind a birch tree, not stopping to pick up some green plums they had dropped.

Prince Andrew turned away with startled haste, unwilling to let them see they had been noticed. He felt sorry for the pretty frightened little girl, was afraid of looking at her, and yet felt an irresistible desire to do so. A new sensation of comfort and relief came over him when, seeing these girls, he realized that other human interests existed entirely apart from his own and just as legitimate as those that consumed him. These girls clearly wanted nothing more passionately than to carry away and eat those green plums without getting caught—and Prince Andrew shared their wish for the success of their enterprise. He couldn't resist looking at them once more. Believing the danger had passed, they sprang from their hiding place and, chirping something in their shrill little voices and holding up their skirts, scampered merrily and quickly on their bare, sunburned feet across the meadow grass.

Prince Andrew felt somewhat refreshed from having ridden off the dusty highway along which the troops were moving. But not far from Bald Hills he came back to the road and overtook his regiment at its halt by the dam of a small pond. It was past one o'clock. The sun, a red ball through the dust, burned and scorched his back unbearably through his black coat. The dust always hung motionless above the buzz of talk from the resting troops. There was no wind. As he crossed the dam, Prince Andrew caught the smell of ooze and freshness from the pond. He longed to get into that water, however dirty it might be, and he glanced at the pond from which came sounds of shrieks and laughter. The small, muddy, green pond had risen visibly more than a foot above the dam, because it was full of naked white bodies of soldiers with sunburned hands, necks, and faces, splashing about in it. All this naked white human flesh, laughing and shrieking, floundered about in that dirty pool like fish stuffed into a watering can, and the suggestion of merriment in that floundering mass made it all the more pitiful.

One fair-haired young soldier of the third company, whom Prince Andrew knew and who had a strap around the calf of one leg, crossed himself, stepped back to get a running start, and plunged into the water; another, a dark noncommissioned officer who was always shaggy, stood waist-deep in the water joyfully flexing his muscular figure and snorted with satisfaction as he poured water over his head with hands blackened to the wrists. There were sounds of men slapping one another, yelling, and spluttering.

Everywhere on the bank, on the dam, and in the pond, there was healthy, white, muscular flesh. The officer Timokhin, with his little red nose, standing on the dam drying himself with a towel, felt embarrassed at seeing the prince but made up his mind to address him anyway.
"It's really nice, your excellency! Wouldn't you like to?" he said.
"It's dirty," replied Prince Andrew, making a face.
"We'll clear it out for you in a minute," said Timokhin, and, still undressed, ran off to clear the men out of the pond.
"The prince wants to bathe."
"What prince? Ours?" said many voices, and the men were in such a hurry to clear out that the prince could barely stop them. He decided he would rather wash himself with water in the barn.

"Flesh, bodies, cannon fodder!" he thought, looking at his own naked body and shuddering—not from cold but from a feeling of disgust and horror he didn't fully understand, aroused by the sight of that immense number of bodies splashing in the dirty pond.
On the seventh of August, Prince Bagration wrote as follows from his quarters at Mikhailovka on the Smolensk road:
Dear Count Alexei Andreevich—(He was writing to Arakcheev but knew the letter would be read by the Emperor, so he weighed every word as carefully as he could.)

I expect the Minister (Barclay de Tolly) has already reported the abandonment of Smolensk to the enemy. It is pitiable and sad, and the whole army is in despair that this most important place has been needlessly abandoned. I, for my part, begged him personally and most urgently, and finally wrote to him, but nothing would persuade him. I swear to you on my honor that Napoleon was in a tighter spot than ever before and might have lost half his army but could not have taken Smolensk. Our troops fought, and are fighting, as never before. With fifteen thousand men I held the enemy at bay for thirty-five hours and beat him; but he would not hold out even for fourteen hours. It is a disgrace, a stain on our army, and as for him, it seems to me he should not go on living. If he reports that our losses were heavy, it is not true; perhaps about four thousand, not more, and not even that; but even were they ten thousand, that's war! But the enemy has lost far more...

What would it have cost him to hold out for another two days? They would have had to retreat on their own, for they had no water for men or horses. He gave me his word he would not retreat, but suddenly sent orders that he was pulling out that night. We cannot fight this way, or we'll soon bring the enemy right to Moscow...

There is a rumor that you are thinking of peace. God forbid that you should make peace after all our sacrifices and such insane retreats! You would turn all Russia against you, and every one of us would be ashamed to wear the uniform. If it has come to this—we must fight as long as Russia stands and as long as there are men able to fight...

One man ought to be in command, not two. Your Minister may perhaps be a good minister, but as a general he is not merely bad but execrable, yet the fate of our whole country has been entrusted to him... I am truly beside myself with frustration; forgive my writing bluntly. It is clear that whoever advocates making peace, and that the Minister should command the army, does not love our sovereign and desires the ruin of us all. So I write to you frankly: call up the militia. For the Minister is leading these visitors of ours straight to Moscow in the most masterly way. The whole army regards the Imperial aide-de-camp Wolzogen with the greatest suspicion. He is said to be more Napoleon's man than ours, and he is forever advising the Minister. I am not merely civil to him but obey him like a corporal, though I am his senior. This is painful, but loving my benefactor and sovereign, I submit. Only I am sorry for the Emperor, that he entrusts our fine army to such a man... Consider that on our retreat we have lost through exhaustion and left in hospitals more than fifteen thousand men, and had we attacked this would not have happened. Tell me, for God's sake, what will Russia—our mother Russia—say to our being so frightened? And why are we abandoning our good and brave Fatherland to such rabble, planting feelings of hatred and shame in all our people? What are we scared of and whom are we afraid of? It is not my fault that the Minister is indecisive, cowardly, dense, slow, and has every bad quality. The whole army weeps over it and curses him...
